title: Idioms and figurative language
objectives: Understand and use high-frequency sawikain (Tagalog idioms) in context
Recognize euphemisms for death, money troubles and other delicate topics
Judge when an idiom fits the situation and register — and when it doesn't
Enjoy and produce light wordplay and humor in conversation

grammar.title: Sawikain: how Tagalog idioms are built
grammar.explanation:
Sawikain are fixed expressions whose meaning can't be computed from the words. Many are compact noun-noun or adjective-noun compounds: balat-sibuyas (onion-skinned) 'overly sensitive'; makapal ang mukha (thick-faced) 'shameless'; magaan ang kamay (light-handed) 'quick to hit'. Blood carries likability: magaan ang dugo ko sa kanya 'I instantly warmed to him', mabigat ang dugo ko sa kanya 'something about him rubs me the wrong way'. Others are mini-scenes: nagbibilang ng poste (counting lampposts) 'jobless, wandering the streets'; itaga mo sa bato (carve it in stone) 'mark my words'; isulat mo sa tubig (write it on water) 'it will never happen'.

Body parts are the favorite raw material: bukas ang palad (open-palmed) 'generous'; mahaba ang dila (long-tongued) 'gossipy'; matigas ang ulo (hard-headed) 'stubborn' — one you likely know already; malikot ang kamay (restless hands) 'thievish'; kumukulo ang dugo (blood is boiling) 'furious'.

Grammatically, most idioms inflect normally: Kumulo ang dugo ko nang marinig ko iyon. But you cannot swap synonyms into them: makapal ang mukha never becomes 'makapal ang pisngi'. Learn each as a frozen unit with its exact wording.

grammar.title: Euphemism: saying the unsayable gently
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog culture prizes indirectness around death, money, and bodily matters, and the language has polished tools for it. Death: instead of namatay, prose and speech prefer pumanaw 'passed away', sumakabilang-buhay 'went to the other life', yumao 'departed', or wala na 'is gone'. You met yumao in Unit 1's reading; now you know its family.

Money troubles: kapos 'short (of funds)', gipit 'in a tight spot', walang datung is slang — the softer standard is medyo kinakapos kami ngayon 'we're a bit short right now'. Asking to borrow: baka naman may maipapautang ka 'perhaps you might have something you could lend' — note how magpautang from Unit 1 reappears wrapped in hedges (baka naman, maipa-).

Other zones: nagdadalang-tao (carrying a person) 'pregnant', may sakit sa isip for mental illness in careful speech, matanda na 'already old' softened to may edad na 'has age already'. Even firing someone hides behind natanggal sa trabaho 'was removed from work' or the borrowed office word na-retrench. Choose euphemisms when the listener is affected personally; plain words belong in news reports and statistics.

grammar.title: When idioms fit — and when they embarrass you
grammar.explanation:
Idioms are register-sensitive in three ways. First, formality: sawikain are at home in conversation, speeches, and feature writing, but out of place in the formal letters of Unit 6 and in technical reports. Itaga mo sa bato belongs in a barbershop debate, not a liham-reklamo.

Second, tone: many idioms are teasing or blunt. Calling someone balat-sibuyas or makapal ang mukha to their face is an insult, however colorful; describing yourself with them (Balat-sibuyas talaga ako, pasensya na) is self-deprecating humor and lands fine. Third, overuse: one idiom per paragraph seasons the dish; five make you sound like a komiks character.

Humor also lives in wordplay on the patterns you know. The affix system invites puns: asked Kumain ka na ba? a joker answers Busog pa ako sa kahapon — 'still full from yesterday'. Proverbs (salawikain, distinct from sawikain!) get twisted for laughs: the sober Kung may tiyaga, may nilaga ('perseverance brings stew') becomes Kung may tiyaga, may nilaga; kung wala, order na lang ng fast food. At B2, your goal is first to catch these plays when natives make them — production can come later.

example.tl: Maraming sawikain ang gumagamit ng mga bahagi ng katawan.
example.en: Many idioms use parts of the body.

example.tl: Paboritong salawikain ng lolo ko: kung may tiyaga, may nilaga.
example.en: My grandfather's favorite proverb: perseverance brings the stew.

example.tl: Mula nang magsara ang pabrika, nagbibilang na lang siya ng poste.
example.en: Since the factory closed, he's just been counting lampposts.

vocab.en: mark my words (lit. carve it in stone)

example.tl: Itaga mo sa bato: babalik ako na may dalang tagumpay.
example.en: Mark my words: I will return carrying success.

example.tl: Huwag kang magbiro sa kanya; balat-sibuyas iyan.
example.en: Don't joke with her; she's onion-skinned.

example.tl: Makapal ang mukha niyang humiram ulit ng pera.
example.en: He shamelessly borrowed money again.

example.tl: Matigas talaga ang ulo ng batang iyan; ayaw makinig.
example.en: That child is really stubborn; he won't listen.

example.tl: Mag-ingat ka sa kanya; mahaba ang dila.
example.en: Be careful around her; she's a gossip.

example.tl: Kilala ang pamilya nila sa pagiging bukas ang palad sa mahihirap.
example.en: Their family is known for being generous to the poor.

example.tl: Kumukulo ang dugo ko tuwing nakikita ko ang ginawa nila.
example.en: My blood boils whenever I see what they did.

vocab.en: instantly likable, easy to get along with

example.tl: Magaan agad ang dugo ko sa bago naming kapitbahay.
example.en: I instantly warmed to our new neighbor.

example.tl: Huwag mong iwanan ang pitaka mo; may malikot ang kamay dito.
example.en: Don't leave your wallet; someone here has sticky fingers.

vocab.en: it will never happen (lit. write it on water)

example.tl: Ang pangako niyang magbabayad? Isulat mo sa tubig.
example.en: His promise to pay? Write it on water.

vocab.en: laborer, working-class person (lit. child of sweat)

example.tl: Mga anak-pawis ang bumuhay sa industriya ng asukal.
example.en: Laborers kept the sugar industry alive.

example.tl: Utak-biya raw ako kasi nakalimutan ko na naman ang susi.
example.en: They said I'm goby-brained because I forgot the key again.

vocab.en: spouse, other half (lit. half of a whole)

example.tl: Ipinakilala niya ang kanyang kabiyak sa mga bisita.
example.en: He introduced his other half to the guests.

vocab.note: pumanaw, pumapanaw, papanaw; gentler than namatay

example.tl: Pumanaw ang kanyang ama noong isang taon.
example.en: His father passed away last year.

vocab.en: to pass on (lit. go to the other life)
vocab.note: completed form most common: sumakabilang-buhay na

example.tl: Sumakabilang-buhay na ang matandang manunulat kaninang umaga.
example.en: The elderly writer passed on this morning.

vocab.en: gone; no longer with us (euphemism for dead)

example.tl: Hindi niya alam na wala na pala ang dati niyang guro.
example.en: He didn't know his former teacher was already gone.

example.tl: Medyo kapos kami ngayong buwan dahil sa matrikula.
example.en: We're a bit short this month because of tuition.

example.tl: Gipit na gipit sila mula nang mawalan ng trabaho ang ama.
example.en: They've been hard-pressed since the father lost his job.

example.tl: Hindi na siya pinapasok sa mabibigat na trabaho dahil nagdadalang-tao siya.
example.en: She's no longer assigned heavy work because she is expecting.

example.tl: Ipinagpaliban ang biyahe dahil may edad na ang kanilang ina.
example.en: The trip was postponed because their mother is getting on in years.

vocab.en: lost one's job, was let go

example.tl: Maraming natanggal sa trabaho nang magsara ang planta.
example.en: Many were let go when the plant closed.

vocab.note: verb: magbiro; nagbibiro lang ako = I'm just joking

example.tl: Huwag mong seryosohin; biro lang iyon.
example.en: Don't take it seriously; it was just a joke.

example.tl: Laging may patawang kuwento ang tiyuhin ko sa hapag.
example.en: My uncle always has a funny story at the table.

example.tl: Puno ng talinghaga ang mga awit ng mga ninuno natin.
example.en: Our ancestors' songs are full of metaphor.

example.tl: Gumamit siya ng patungkol na di-tuwiran sa halip na banggitin ang pangalan.
example.en: She used an indirect reference instead of mentioning the name.

dialogue.title: Sa barberya
dialogue.context: At the neighborhood barbershop, Mang Caloy the barber and his customer Dado trade news and idioms while a haircut proceeds.

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Balita ko, natanggal sa trabaho ang pamangkin mo. Kumusta na siya?
lines.en: I heard your nephew lost his job. How is he?

lines.speaker: Dado
lines.tl: Ayun, tatlong buwan nang nagbibilang ng poste. Pero itaga mo sa bato, Caloy: makakabangon din ang batang iyon.
lines.en: Well, three months now counting lampposts. But mark my words, Caloy: that kid will get back on his feet.

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Naniniwala ako. Magaan ang dugo ko sa pamangkin mo — masipag at magalang.
lines.en: I believe it. I've always liked your nephew — hardworking and respectful.

lines.speaker: Dado
lines.tl: Kaso medyo balat-sibuyas. Noong tinukso siya ng mga pinsan niya tungkol sa trabaho, hindi umimik nang dalawang araw.
lines.en: Trouble is he's a bit onion-skinned. When his cousins teased him about the job, he didn't speak for two days.

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Hay, kabataan. E ang dati niyang amo, ano'ng nangyari?
lines.en: Ah, young people. And his former boss, what happened there?

lines.speaker: Dado
lines.tl: Huwag na nating pag-usapan. Kumukulo ang dugo ko sa taong iyon. Makapal ang mukhang nangako ng separation pay — isulat mo na lang daw sa tubig.
lines.en: Let's not talk about him. My blood boils at that man. He shamelessly promised separation pay — might as well write it on water.

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Naku. Buti na lang bukas ang palad ng lola ninyo; siya muna ang bumubuhay sa bata, di ba?
lines.en: Goodness. Good thing your grandmother is open-handed; she's supporting the kid for now, right?

lines.speaker: Dado
lines.tl: Oo, kahit may edad na siya at kapos din minsan. Kaya nga nag-aapply na ang bata kahit saan.
lines.en: Yes, even though she's getting on in years and sometimes short herself. That's why the kid is applying everywhere.

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Sabihin mo sa kanya, kung may tiyaga, may nilaga.
lines.en: Tell him: perseverance brings the stew.

lines.speaker: Dado
lines.tl: Sasabihin ko: kung may tiyaga, may nilaga — at kung may gunting, may gupit. O, bilisan mo na, Caloy!
lines.en: I'll tell him: perseverance brings the stew — and where there are scissors, there's a haircut. Now hurry it up, Caloy!

lines.speaker: Mang Caloy
lines.tl: Ha! Nagbibiro ka na naman. Tapos na, pare. Libre na ang kuwento.
lines.en: Ha! Joking again. All done, friend. The stories were free.

reading.title: Ang wikang hindi mo mababasa sa diksyunaryo
reading.tl:
Marunong ka na bang mag-Tagalog? Subukan natin. Ano ang ibig sabihin ng "nagbibilang ng poste"? Kung ang sagot mo ay "isang taong nagbibilang ng mga poste sa kalye," marunong ka ngang magsalin — pero hindi ka pa marunong makinig sa puso ng wika.

Ang sawikain ang bahagi ng wikang hindi kayang buksan ng diksyunaryo lamang. Kapag sinabi ng iyong kapitbahay na "balat-sibuyas" ang kanyang manugang, wala itong kinalaman sa gulay; ibig sabihin, madaling masaktan. Kapag ibinulong sa iyo na "mahaba ang dila" ng isang kasamahan, hindi ito obserbasyon tungkol sa anatomiya kundi babala: mag-ingat ka sa mga sinasabi mo.

Bakit mahalaga ito sa isang nag-aaral ng Tagalog? Sapagkat ang mga Pilipino ay bihirang magsalita nang tuwiran tungkol sa mabibigat na paksa. Sa halip na sabihing "namatay ang kanyang ama," mas madalas mong maririnig na "pumanaw" o "sumakabilang-buhay na." Sa halip na "wala akong pera," ang sasabihin ay "medyo kapos ako ngayon." Ang di-tuwirang pananalita ay hindi pagsisinungaling; ito ay paraan ng pag-iingat sa damdamin ng kapwa.

Gayunpaman, may tamang lugar ang lahat. Ang sawikain ay pampalasa ng usapan at talumpati, ngunit hindi ito nababagay sa liham-reklamo o sa ulat ng negosyo. At tandaan: ang idyomang ginamit sa maling pagkakataon ay parang asin sa kape — hindi masama ang sangkap, mali lamang ang timpla. Kaya makinig muna nang matagal bago gumamit. Itaga mo sa bato: darating ang araw na ang mga poste ay bibilangin mo na rin — bilang biro, hindi bilang kahulugan.
reading.en:
Do you know Tagalog now? Let's test it. What does "counting lampposts" mean? If your answer is "a person counting the posts on the street," then you indeed know how to translate — but you don't yet know how to listen to the heart of the language.

Idioms are the part of a language that a dictionary alone cannot unlock. When your neighbor says her son-in-law is "onion-skinned," it has nothing to do with vegetables; it means easily hurt. When someone whispers that a colleague is "long-tongued," it is not an observation about anatomy but a warning: watch what you say.

Why does this matter to a learner of Tagalog? Because Filipinos rarely speak directly about heavy subjects. Instead of saying "his father died," you will more often hear "passed away" or "crossed to the other life." Instead of "I have no money," what you'll hear is "I'm a bit short right now." Indirect speech is not lying; it is a way of protecting other people's feelings.

Nevertheless, everything has its proper place. Idioms are the seasoning of conversation and speeches, but they do not suit a complaint letter or a business report. And remember: an idiom used on the wrong occasion is like salt in coffee — the ingredient isn't bad, only the mixture is wrong. So listen for a long time before using them. Mark my words: the day will come when you too will count lampposts — as a joke, not as a definition.

gloss.en: connection, relevance (walang kinalaman = nothing to do with)

exercises.prompt: Tatlong buwan na siyang nagbibilang ng poste. What does this mean?
choices: He has been working for the electric company for three months.
He has been jobless for three months.
He has been counting his savings for three months.
He has walked to work for three months.
exercises.explain: Nagbibilang ng poste (counting lampposts) is the idiom for being jobless and idle — someone with nothing to do but wander the streets.

exercises.prompt: Your friend says: 'Itaga mo sa bato: papasa ako sa bar exam.' What are they doing?
choices: Asking you to carve their name on a stone
Making an emphatic promise — 'mark my words'
Expressing doubt about the exam
Telling you a proverb about patience
exercises.explain: Itaga mo sa bato (carve it in stone) prefaces an emphatic vow or prediction: 'mark my words'.

exercises.prompt: Huwag kang magbiro tungkol sa timbang niya; ___-sibuyas siya. (overly sensitive)
exercises.hint: an onion has thin layers of this
exercises.explain: Balat-sibuyas 'onion-skinned' describes someone easily hurt by teasing — thin-skinned, layer by layer.

exercises.prompt: Which is a euphemistic way to say someone died?
choices: Sumakabilang-buhay na siya.
Patay na patay siya sa kanya.
Namatayan siya ng ilaw.
Mataas na ang lagnat niya.
exercises.explain: Sumakabilang-buhay 'went to the other life' is a standard euphemism, like pumanaw and wala na. Patay na patay sa kanya actually means 'has a huge crush on her'!

exercises.prompt: Pasensya na, hindi muna ako makakapagpahiram. Medyo ___ kami ngayong buwan. (short of money — gentle word)
exercises.hint: the soft way to say funds are lacking
exercises.explain: Kapos 'short' (or gipit 'in a tight spot') is the polite way to admit money trouble without the bluntness of walang pera.

exercises.tl: Kumulo ang dugo ko nang malaman kong makapal pala ang mukha niyang humingi ulit ng tulong.
exercises.prompt: How does the speaker feel, and about what?
choices: Furious, because the person shamelessly asked for help again.
Amused, because the person told a funny joke again.
Feverish, because of an illness.
Grateful, because the person helped them again.
exercises.explain: Kumulo ang dugo ko = 'my blood boiled' (fury); makapal ang mukha = 'shameless'. Two body idioms stacked in one sentence.

exercises.prompt: Bukas ang palad ng pamilyang iyan sa sinumang nangangailangan.
exercises.answer: That family is generous to anyone in need.
accept: That family is generous to anyone in need
That family is open-handed to anyone who needs help
That family gives generously to whoever is in need
exercises.explain: Bukas ang palad (open-palmed) = generous. Sinumang nangangailangan = 'anyone in need' — kahit-style indefinite from Unit 4's family.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a euphemism appropriately?
choices: Sa liham-reklamo: 'Itaga ninyo sa bato, magrereklamo ako!'
Sa kausap na namatayan: 'Nakikiramay ako sa pagpanaw ng inyong ina.'
Sa ulat ng gobyerno: 'Nagbibilang ng poste ang 5% ng populasyon.'
Sa pulong ng negosyo: 'Utak-biya ang ating mga kliyente.'
exercises.explain: Condolences call for the euphemism pagpanaw 'passing'. Idioms are wrong in complaint letters and statistics, and utak-biya is an insult — disastrous in a business meeting.

exercises.prompt: Be careful what you tell her — she's long-tongued.
exercises.answer: Mag-ingat ka sa sinasabi mo sa kanya — mahaba ang dila niya.
accept: Mag-ingat ka sa sinasabi mo sa kanya — mahaba ang dila niya
Mag-ingat ka sa sinasabi mo sa kanya, mahaba ang dila niya
Ingatan mo ang sinasabi mo sa kanya dahil mahaba ang dila niya
exercises.explain: Mahaba ang dila (long-tongued) = gossipy. The idiom keeps its exact wording; you inflect only the possessor (niya).

exercises.prompt: A colleague announces: 'Nagdadalang-tao na pala si Weng!' What is the news?
choices: Weng is carrying heavy boxes.
Weng is pregnant.
Weng has adopted a child.
Weng is babysitting.
exercises.explain: Nagdadalang-tao (carrying a person) is the respectful euphemism for pregnancy; buntis is the plain term.

exercises.tl: Magaan agad ang dugo ko sa bago naming katrabaho, pero sabi nila, medyo matigas daw ang ulo.
exercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the new coworker?
choices: They instantly liked the coworker, though others say the coworker is stubborn.
The coworker has low blood pressure and headaches.
They disliked the coworker, who others say is very humble.
The coworker instantly liked the speaker but is very shy.
exercises.explain: Magaan ang dugo ko sa kanya = 'I instantly warmed to them'; matigas ang ulo = 'stubborn'; daw marks it as hearsay from others.

exercises.prompt: His promise to change? Write it on water.
exercises.answer: Ang pangako niyang magbabago? Isulat mo sa tubig.
accept: Ang pangako niyang magbabago? Isulat mo sa tubig
Ang pangako niya na magbabago? Isulat mo sa tubig
Ang pangako niyang magbabago ay isulat mo na lang sa tubig
exercises.explain: Isulat mo sa tubig (write it on water) dismisses a promise as worthless — words that vanish as soon as they're written. Note isulat, the i- verb from Unit 1, frozen inside the idiom.
